name: Venera 13
payload: Venera 13 flyby bus and descent lander (4V-1)
significance: Venera 13 carried a lander that reached the surface of Venus east of Phoebe Regio and kept working for just over two hours under about 89 times Earth's air pressure and a temperature near 457 °C. It returned the first colour pictures of the Venusian surface, showing flat, layered rock and soil, and drilled a surface sample that its onboard X-ray fluorescence spectrometer analysed, finding a composition like Earth's alkaline basalts. Its flyby bus relayed the lander's data as it passed the planet and then continued into solar orbit, where its gamma-ray instruments kept observing. Together with its twin Venera 14, it set the benchmark for surviving and working on the Venusian surface that no later lander has exceeded.
statusNote: Direct Earth->Venus transfer; drawn as a single arc ending at Venus on the landing date. The lander touched down on 1982-03-01 (about 03:57 UTC) at 7.5°S, 303°E and survived 2 h 7 min (127 min). The bus flew past Venus at the same time, relaying lander data, then continued into solar orbit (not drawn: single-arc flights end at arrival). Launch date and lander duration and location: NSSDCA (Venus chronology, https://nssdc.gsfc.nasa.gov/planetary/chronology_venus.html; lander image catalog pages YG06847/YG06848). Landing clock time from secondary sources (Wikipedia). No JPL Horizons ephemeris exists for Venera 13. Path calculated, not measured (drawn dashed): no tracking data for this spacecraft is publicly archived (JPL Horizons has no ephemeris for it), so the path is a two-body transfer calculated between the published launch, flyby and arrival times. Arcs calculated this way for modern direct flights fall within about 0.002 AU of their real Horizons trajectories.
